newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists apologise for Stalinist purges. [CORRECTED 14:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: French Communists apologise for Stalinist purges. [CORRECTED 14:40 GMT]

text.p: France's Communists, eager to shed the last remnants of their Stalinist past now that they are in government, have publicly apologised to former party officials purged in the 1960s for denouncing Stalin's crimes.

Party leader Robert Hue travelled on Sunday to the eastern France home of one of the most famous victims of the purges, 83-year-old Maurice Kriegel-Valrimont, to voice regrets and pledge a rewrite of the party's history.

"Settling differences by unconditionally espousing views said to be infallible and attacking comrades on their integrity as human beings was an immense mess for all Communists," Hue told what was billed as a "brotherly meeting" of a few hundred party members.

He embraced Kriegel-Valrimont and was photographed shielding him from a downpour under his umbrella, a fitting symbol of rehabilitation for the former hero of anti-Nazi Resistance who said that the public reconciliation between a party chief and "a former damned" was unprecedented.

The purges stemmed from the French party's refusal to condemn repression of the anti-Soviet uprising in Hungary and to endorse the condemnation of Stalin's crimes made at the crucial 20th congress of the Soviet Communist Party in 1956.
Some Communists left the party while others became dissidents.
"Yes, Stalinism left a deep and long-lasting mark on the party. Silencing the disclosures of the 20th Congress...had heavy consequences," Hue said.

Kriegel-Valrimont was sacked from the central committee in 1961. Hue also mentioned the late Laurent Casanova and Marcel Servin who were barred from official duties in 1961 but remained party members, and Charles Tillon who was punished in 1953 for "fractionary activities" -- a classic accusation in Stalinist purges.
The party rehabilitated Tillon in 1957 and sacked him again in 1970 together with his wife Raymonde, a survivor of Nazi death camps.
"There were -- we must say it even if there is bitterness -- genuine trials against them in which they were made to silently submit," Hue said.
He said the purges had prevented the Communists from gaining strength in French society and said he favoured historians being given all means to explore the party's history.
The Communists, who struck an election alliance with the Socialists, returned to the cabinet for the first time in 13 years this month after the left won June 1 parliamentary elections.
Communists were given the transport, sports and tourism portfolios in the new cabinet.

Since he took over from Stalinist veteran Georges Marchais as national secretary of the party three years ago, the rotund 50-year-old Hue has sought to get rid of an embarrassing legacy and bury the party's image as one of the most hardline in the West.
Distancing himself from Marchais' unflinching support for former Soviet regimes, he called them "perversions of Communism".
Hue has apparently managed to halt the long decline of a party whose public support stood at around 25 percent when Marchais took over in 1972.
Hue won 8.6 percent of the votes in the 1995 presidential election, and Communists won 9.9 percent of the votes and 38 of the National Assembly's 577 seats in the last parliamentary election.
